---
title: The Slow Hive
url: https://example.com/p/the-slow-hive
---

I kept bees for eleven years before I understood that a hive is not a machine for making honey. For most of that time I treated it like one. I opened the boxes every week, counted frames, and worried when the numbers dipped. The bees tolerated me the way the sea tolerates a swimmer.

What changed was a bad winter. Three of my five colonies died, and the two that lived were the ones I had neglected. I had been too busy that autumn to fuss over them. They sealed their own cracks with propolis, clustered early, and came out in March thin but whole.

A colony knows its own temperature better than I ever will. When I open the box in cold weather I am not checking on the bees; I am letting the heat out of their house. The urge to inspect is mostly an urge to feel useful.

I think this is true of a lot of care. We confuse attention with interference. The gardener who digs up the seed to see if it has sprouted has killed the thing she wanted to watch.

There is a second lesson in the hive that took me longer. Bees do not have a leader in the way we imagine. The queen lays eggs; she does not give orders. Decisions — where to swarm, when to raise a new queen — emerge from thousands of small votes, a scout dancing harder for a better site. A hive is a conversation that never ends.

When I started running the community garden I tried to be the queen we imagine instead of the one that exists. I made the plans, assigned the beds, and resented everyone who didn't follow them. The garden only started working when I stopped deciding and started hosting: a shared table, a seed swap, a notice board where anyone could propose a project. Good decisions came from the edges, the way the best nest sites are found by scouts nobody sent.

So now I try to keep two rules. Leave the box closed unless you have a reason. And when a group needs a direction, build the dance floor, not the throne.
